hints: Focus on the oxidation number of chlorine before and after the reaction, not just on the names of the products.
Write the equation for cold $\text{NaOH}$: $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, and assign oxidation numbers to each chlorine.
Check if the starting oxidation number of 0 splits into both a higher and a lower value, which is the hallmark of disproportionation.
walkthrough:
**Recall what cold NaOH does to chlorine**

Chlorine reacts with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide to make chloride, chlorate(I) and water. This is a very famous reaction to learn.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Track the oxidation number of chlorine**

Start with $\text{Cl}_2$. Each Cl atom is in an element, so its oxidation number is 0.

In products:
$$\text{Cl in NaCl} = -1, \quad \text{Cl in NaClO} = +1$$

**Spot oxidation and reduction together**

Going from 0 to -1 is a decrease in oxidation number, so reduction. Going from 0 to +1 is an increase, so oxidation.

Since the same element $\text{Cl}_2$ is both oxidised and reduced, this is called disproportionation.

options.A: Correct. Chlorine starts at 0 in Cl2, then goes to -1 in NaCl (reduced) and to +1 in NaClO (oxidised). One element doing both is disproportionation.
options.B: Not correct. Oxidation numbers clearly change from 0 to -1 and +1, so redox definitely happens. This choice ignores the change in oxidation state.
options.C: Not correct. It is true that Cl is oxidised to +1 in NaClO, but it misses that Cl is also reduced to -1 in NaCl. Students who only look at NaClO pick this trap.
options.D: Not correct. It is true that Cl is reduced to -1 in NaCl, but it misses that Cl is also oxidised to +1 in NaClO. Students who only look at NaCl pick this trap.
